question: How can structured regression forms (additive models, trees, MARS, PRIM, HME) sidestep the curse of dimensionality, and at what cost in misspecification?
contributions: Describes five related techniques: generalized additive models, trees, MARS, PRIM, hierarchical mixtures of experts.

limits: Additive models fit all predictors, which is not feasible or desirable with many predictors (9.1.3); BRUTO, COSSO, SpAM and boosting named as remedies.
Trees: high variance (small data changes change splits), non-smooth surface, difficulty capturing additive structure (9.2.4).
Many-level categorical predictors cause severe overfitting in tree splits; such variables should be avoided (9.2.4).
PRIM has no simple way to handle k>2 classes; no binary-tree description makes the rule collection harder to interpret (9.3).
MARS forward cost NM^3 + pM^2N is prohibitive when M is a reasonable fraction of N (9.7); MARS does worse on neural-network-like high-order interaction data (R2 0.79).
No method is known for choosing HME tree topology; EM can be slow, big HMEs costly (9.5, 9.7).
MARS simulation uses only 5 replicates per scenario; spam results use one split with no repeated-split variance, only a binomial SE estimate (about 0.01 for differences near 0.9) in 9.2.5.
Missing-data methods assume MCAR; MAR/MCAR must be judged from the collection process (9.6).
2009 text: boosting (Ch. 10) is recommended for large problems; random forests and gradient boosting later dominated tree use.
practices: Use cubic smoothing splines with df_j set by trace[S_j]-1 to calibrate smoothness; df_j=1 gives linear terms (9.1.1, 9.1.2).
After fitting an additive model, check whether interactions help, manually via products or via MARS (9.1.2).
Grow a large tree to minimum node size (say 5), then prune by cost-complexity with alpha chosen by 5- or 10-fold CV (9.2.2).
Do not stop splitting on a small gain; a worthless split may enable a good one below (9.2.2).
Grow classification trees with Gini index or cross-entropy; use misclassification rate to guide pruning (9.2.3).
For a binary outcome, order categorical levels by proportion in class 1 and split as ordered, which is optimal (9.2.4).
Handle unequal losses in two-class trees by weighting observations in class k by L_{k,1-k}, better than only changing the node rule (9.2.5).
Handle missing predictors in trees with a 'missing' category or surrogate splits (9.2.4).
Prefer binary splits over multiway; multiway fragment the data (9.2.4).
Use ROC and AUC to summarise sensitivity/specificity trade-off, but do not use the c-statistic to judge the added value of one predictor (9.2.5).
Use PRIM with alpha 0.05 or 0.10, peeling then pasting, and CV plus analyst judgement to pick box size (9.3).
Use MARS with GCV (c=3, c=2 for additive), cap interaction degree for interpretability, each input at most once per product (9.4).

Check whether data are missing at random before imputing; with moderate feature dependence impute from a predictive model, with CART as engine; use multiple imputation to gauge extra uncertainty (9.6).

code.snippet: Backfitting: 1. alpha_hat = mean(y), f_j = 0. 2. Cycle j=1..p,...: f_j <- S_j[{y_i - alpha_hat - sum_{k!=j} f_k(x_ik)}]; f_j <- f_j - (1/N) sum_i f_j(x_ij); until f_j change less than threshold.

Local scoring: alpha_hat=log[ybar/(1-ybar)], f_j=0. Iterate: eta_i=alpha+sum f_j(x_ij), p_i=1/(1+exp(-eta_i)); z_i = eta_i + (y_i-p_i)/(p_i(1-p_i)); w_i = p_i(1-p_i); weighted backfit z on x with w_i.
min_{j,s} [ min_{c1} sum_{xi in R1(j,s)} (yi-c1)^2 + min_{c2} sum_{xi in R2(j,s)} (yi-c2)^2 ]

PRIM: peel proportion alpha (0.05 or 0.10) from the face giving the highest remaining box mean until ~10 observations remain; paste (expand faces that raise the mean); choose box by CV; remove box data and repeat.
GCV(lambda) = sum_i (yi - f_lambda(xi))^2 / (1 - M(lambda)/N)^2, M(lambda)=r+cK, c=3
